title: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
summary: Train a GPT to predict several future tokens per position: the parallel-heads design of Gloeckle et al., why it helps, DeepSeek-V3's sequential MTP modules, and reusing heads to decode faster.
outcomes: Explain how the multi-token loss adds n targets per position without changing the input or context
Compute the loss and peak logit memory of an n-head model and the memory saved by per-head backward passes
Explain the choice-point and mutual-information arguments and when MTP helps or hurts
Trace DeepSeek-V3's sequential MTP module: its inputs, index alignment and weighted loss
Compute expected tokens per forward pass for self-speculative decoding from an acceptance rate

lessons.title: From one target per position to n targets per position

blocks.md: In the GPT you built, every position $t$ of a training sequence produces one prediction: a distribution over the vocabulary for the **next** token $x_{t+1}$. The loss is the average cross-entropy of those predictions, and teacher forcing feeds the true prefix at every position. This is next-token prediction, and it is the objective behind GPT and Llama.

Gloeckle et al. (FAIR at Meta, 2024) argue that this objective is an inefficient teacher. Each position is graded only on what comes immediately next, so the model can drive the loss down by latching on to **local** patterns. Decisions whose consequences show up several tokens later (which function to call, which branch of an argument to take) get no more weight than a choice between synonyms.

**Multi-token prediction (MTP)** changes the question asked at each position. Instead of only the next token, the model predicts the next $n$ tokens $x_{t+1}, \dots, x_{t+n}$, each from the same context $x_{1:t}$. The extra predictions are an **auxiliary task**: a second training signal added to the main one, used to shape the shared representation. Let us see what that does to the training targets on a tiny sequence.

blocks.title: Targets per position: n = 1 versus n = 3

scenes.caption: An 8-token training sequence. Row labels name what each prediction head would be asked for; nothing is predicted yet.
Next-token prediction: position t is graded on token t+1. Seven positions have a target, so the sequence contributes 7 loss terms.
Add a second head for token t+2. Position 3 ('sat') must now also predict 'the'. Six more targets: 13 loss terms from the same 8 tokens.
With n = 3, each position answers three questions from one context. Head i has 8 - i targets, so 7 + 6 + 5 = 18 loss terms. Same data, denser supervision.

Read one column: at position 3 the model sees only 'the cat sat' and must commit to 'on', 'the', 'mat'. It cannot see the tokens it predicts, so the representation at t must carry information about where the text is going.

blocks.caption: The multi-token loss of Gloeckle et al.: the sum over positions of n cross-entropy terms, one per future offset. With n = 1 it is the ordinary next-token loss.

blocks.md: Two clarifications prevent most confusion. First, the $n$ predictions at position $t$ are made **in parallel** from the same context; head 2 never sees head 1's guess. That is why the loss is a plain sum of separate log-probabilities, not a joint probability of the $n$-token block. Second, this changes training only. At inference time the simplest use is to keep just the next-token head and decode exactly like any GPT.

Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 5 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

blocks.prompt: If MTP adds more loss terms per sequence, does it also increase the number of tokens the model is trained on?
blocks.reveal: No. The training corpus and the number of forward passes over it are unchanged. MTP extracts **more targets from each position** of the same data. DeepSeek-V3's report puts it as 'densifies the training signals'. Whether denser signals actually help is an empirical question, which lesson 3 answers with numbers.

blocks.md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

blocks.question: A 10-token sequence is trained with n = 4 independent future heads. How many loss terms does it contribute (count head i as having 10 - i targets)?
options: 9, because only the next-token head counts
40, because each of 10 positions has 4 targets
36, because 4 x 9
blocks.explain: Head 1 has targets for positions 1 to 9, head 2 for positions 1 to 8, and so on: 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 = 30. Positions near the end have fewer valid future tokens, so the count is not simply 10 x 4.

blocks.question: During training, what does the head that predicts x(t+3) receive as input at position t?
options: The shared representation of the prefix x(1..t) only
The prefix plus head 1's and head 2's predicted tokens
The true tokens x(t+1) and x(t+2), via teacher forcing
The whole sequence, with future tokens masked out after the loss
blocks.explain: In the Gloeckle design all heads read the same trunk output for the prefix ending at t and predict in parallel. No head sees other heads' guesses or any token after t. (DeepSeek-V3 makes a different choice, covered in lesson 4.)

lessons.title: Shared trunk, n heads, and the memory trick that keeps it cheap

blocks.md: Gloeckle et al. split the transformer into three parts. A **shared trunk** $f_s$ (most of the layers) turns the context $x_{1:t}$ into a hidden state $z_t$. There are $n$ **independent heads** $f_{h_i}$, each a single transformer layer. Finally one **shared unembedding** $f_u$ maps a head's output to vocabulary logits.

blocks.caption: Head 1 is the next-token head. Every head reads the same trunk output and uses the same unembedding matrix.

blocks.title: Gloeckle et al. architecture with n = 4 heads

scenes.caption: Start from a plain GPT: context in, trunk, one output layer, a next-token distribution.
Add three more heads on the same trunk output z_t. Each head is one transformer layer, so heads can specialize to their offset.
All heads share one unembedding matrix (size d x V), so the expensive vocabulary projection is not copied n times.
Compute-matched comparison: when n - 1 head layers are added, n - 1 layers are removed from the trunk, so the MTP model has the same parameter count as its baseline.
At inference, the default is to run trunk and head 1 only, which is an ordinary next-token model. Heads 2 to 4 are dimmed: optional extras.

blocks.md: A tiny worked example shows what one position contributes to the loss. Take a 5-token vocabulary {sat, on, the, mat, cat}, context 'the cat', and $n = 3$, so the targets are 'sat', 'on', 'the'. Each head produces its own logits; the shared unembedding is already folded into them here.

blocks.title: One position, three heads: softmax and loss

scenes.caption: Head 1, logits [2.0, 0.5, 0.1, -1.0, 0.3]. Softmax gives p(sat) = 0.623, so the loss term is -ln 0.623 = 0.473.
Head 2 (two steps ahead), logits [0.2, 1.5, 0.4, -0.5, 0.0]. p(on) = 0.509, loss 0.675. Less confident, as expected further out.
Head 3, logits [0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 0.6, 0.2]. p(the) = 0.331, loss 1.106. This position contributes 0.473 + 0.675 + 1.106 = 2.254 to the summed loss.

blocks.md: The cost problem is the unembedding. Vocabulary size $V$ (32k in their token-level runs) is far larger than the hidden size $d$, so the logits tensor and its gradient dominate memory. A naive implementation materializes logits and gradients for all $n$ heads at once, peak memory $O(nV + d)$ per token, which shrinks the batch size you can fit.

Their fix reorders the computation. Run the trunk forward once. Then for each head in turn: forward the head, compute its loss, backward through the head, and **add** the gradient into a buffer at the trunk output, then free that head's logits. Only the $d$-dimensional trunk gradient lives across heads. After the last head, run one backward through the trunk. Peak memory drops to $O(V + d)$.

blocks.title: Forward and backward order for n = 2 heads

scenes.caption: Step 1: one forward pass through the shared trunk produces z for every position.
Head 1 runs forward, computes its loss and immediately backpropagates to the trunk output. Its V-sized logits exist only during this window.
Head 1's logits are freed before head 2 starts. Head 2's gradient is added into the same d-sized buffer at the trunk output.
Finally one backward pass through the trunk with the accumulated gradient. At no moment are two heads' logits alive together, so peak memory is that of one head.

blocks.code:
z = trunk(x)                      # [B, T, d], forward once
z_leaf = z.detach().requires_grad_()
for i, head in enumerate(heads, start=1):
    logits = unembed(head(z_leaf))   # [B, T, V], only one head alive
    loss_i = F.cross_entropy(
        logits[:, :-i].flatten(0, 1),
        x[:, i:].flatten())
    loss_i.backward()                # grads add up in z_leaf.grad
    del logits                       # free V-sized tensors now
z.backward(z_leaf.grad)              # one backward through the trunk
blocks.caption: Sketch of the sequential order in PyTorch style (not the authors' code). Detaching z lets each head backpropagate only to the trunk output, where gradients accumulate.

blocks.md: How big is the saving? A simplified estimate: a micro-batch of 8 sequences x 4096 tokens with $V$ = 32,000, logits and their gradients in bf16 (2 bytes each). One head's logits take 2.10 GB and its gradient another 2.10 GB, 4.19 GB together. Holding all heads at once would need 8.39 GB for $n = 2$ and 16.78 GB for $n = 4$; the sequential order needs 4.19 GB for any $n$. (Real frameworks often upcast logits to fp32, which doubles these numbers.)

Measured cost: relative to next-token training, the paper's Table S5 lists training time of 1.02 to 1.07 for n = 2 and 1.07 to 1.22 for n = 4 across 0.3B to 13B models. The authors attribute this overhead to losing FSDP's overlap of weight communication and compute during separate per-head backward passes, and say a better implementation can remove it.

blocks.question: A colleague implements MTP with n = 4 by summing four head losses and calling backward once. Training now runs out of memory at the old batch size. What is the most likely cause?
options: The trunk activations are stored four times
All four heads' V-sized logits and gradients are alive at once, so peak memory grows with n
The shared unembedding matrix is copied four times
Cross-entropy needs fp64 when several losses are summed
blocks.explain: Summing losses and calling backward once keeps every head's logits in the graph until the end, so logit memory scales as nV per token. Running forward and backward per head and accumulating the d-sized gradient at the trunk keeps only one head's logits alive.

blocks.question: In the paper's comparisons, a 4-token model and its next-token baseline have equal parameter counts. How?
options: The 4-token model uses a smaller vocabulary
The heads are linear layers with no parameters worth counting
Three layers are removed from the trunk to pay for the three extra head layers
The baseline is trained on four times fewer tokens
blocks.explain: Each head is one transformer layer. Adding n - 1 extra head layers and removing n - 1 trunk layers keeps the total equal, so gains cannot be explained by extra parameters.

lessons.title: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not

blocks.md: Why would extra targets make the next-token head better? The paper offers two arguments, which the authors label as speculation, plus a body of experiments. Start with the arguments, because they also predict where MTP should help most.

**Choice points.** Most tokens in code or prose are easy given the prefix, but a few are **choice points**: decisions that change what follows (which loop to write, what the answer is). Under teacher forcing, a next-token model is graded on a choice point once. With $n$-token prediction, the positions just before the choice point are also asked to predict the choice and its consequences, so the decision shows up in many more loss terms.

blocks.title: Counting loss terms that touch a choice point (n = 3)

scenes.caption: A sequence where every transition is easy except 5 to A, the choice point (after the paper's Figure 9). Tokens after A follow from A.
Next-token prediction grades the choice once: position 5 predicting A.
With n = 3, position 5 must also predict B and C, which depend on the choice of A: 3 terms from position 5.
Position 4 predicts 5, A, B: two terms depend on the choice. Position 3 predicts 4, 5, A: one term. Total 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 = n(n+1)/2.
An easy transition such as 2 to 3 is predicted once per head, n = 3 times. So the choice point gets 6 / 3 = 2 = (n+1)/2 times more relative weight than under next-token training.

blocks.caption: From the paper's Appendix L.3, in a simplified model of teacher-forced training on optimal trajectories. For n = 4 the ratio is 10 / 4 = 2.5.

blocks.md: **Mutual information.** Let $X$ be the next token and $Y$ the one after, both given the context. Next-token training at this position targets the entropy $H(X)$; 2-token training targets $H(X) + H(Y)$. Decomposing both:

blocks.tex: H(X) = H(X \mid Y) + I(X;Y), \qquad H(X) + H(Y) = H(X \mid Y) + 2\,I(X;Y) + H(Y \mid X)
blocks.caption: The term H(Y | X) is learned again at the next position anyway, so the new emphasis is that the mutual information I(X;Y) counts twice.

blocks.md: A worked example, computed exactly. Suppose the next token is 'def' or 'class' with probability 0.5 each, and the token after depends on it: p(def, foo) = 0.4, p(def, bar) = 0.1, p(class, Foo) = 0.45, p(class, bar) = 0.05. Then $H(X)$ = 1.000 bit, $H(Y)$ = 1.458, $H(X,Y)$ = 1.595, so $I(X;Y)$ = 0.862, $H(X \mid Y)$ = 0.138 and $H(Y \mid X)$ = 0.595. Check: 0.138 + 2(0.862) + 0.595 = 2.458 = $H(X) + H(Y)$. Most of what is uncertain about $X$ is information that is *relevant to what comes next*, and the 2-token loss doubles exactly that part.
These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

**What the experiments show** (models trained on code from scratch, compute-matched):

- Benefits grow with scale. Across six sizes from 0.3B to 13B, MTP is worse than the baseline for small models and better at large ones. The 13B model solves 12% more HumanEval and 17% more MBPP problems than the next-token model (relative gains).
- The best $n$ depends on data. At 7B on 200B tokens of code with a 32k vocabulary, $n = 4$ won on MBPP and HumanEval; $n = 6$ led on APPS/Intro. For byte-level models, $n = 8$ was best.
- Natural language is mixed. At 7B on 200B tokens, $n = 2$ matched the baseline on six multiple-choice benchmarks and $n = 4$ regressed slightly, while both improved summarization ROUGE-L.

scenes.caption: MBPP pass@1. n = 4 reaches 33.8 versus 30.0 for the next-token baseline, +3.8 points. Going further to 6 or 8 gives some of it back.
HumanEval pass@1. n = 4 is again best (24.0 versus 22.8), but n = 6 and n = 8 fall below the baseline. More lookahead is not automatically better.
APPS/Intro pass@100 tells a different story: n = 6 leads with 22.7 versus 17.4. The paper concludes the optimal window likely depends on the data distribution.

blocks.prompt: The induction experiment trains tiny models (1M to 1B non-embedding parameters) on children's stories with n = 1 and n = 2. Which way do you expect the gap to go as models get larger?
blocks.reveal: 2-token prediction **vastly** improved induction (copying a pattern seen earlier in the context) for models of 30M non-embedding parameters and below, but the advantage **disappeared** around 100M. The authors read this as MTP helping a capability form; once it has formed, the task becomes a local next-token problem. This echoes the bigger picture with a twist: on the hardest generative benchmarks, gains appear only at larger scale.

blocks.md: MTP reweights training toward decisions that matter for the continuation. It helps most on generative tasks such as code, at larger model sizes, with n tuned to the data; it is not a free win on every benchmark.

blocks.question: With n = 6, how much more relative weight does a choice point get than an inconsequential transition, under the paper's simplified counting?
options: 6 times
21 times
3.5 times
1 time, since all tokens are weighted equally by cross-entropy
blocks.explain: A choice point is touched by 1 + 2 + ... + 6 = 21 loss terms, an inconsequential step by 6. Relative to next-token training the ratio is 21 / 6 = 3.5 = (n+1)/2.

blocks.question: A team training a 300M-parameter code model switches to 4-token prediction because 'the paper showed +12% on HumanEval'. What is the main risk?
options: None: MTP helps at every scale
Small models were worse than the baseline in the paper; the gains appeared at larger sizes
4-token prediction makes inference 4x slower
HumanEval cannot be evaluated with MTP models
blocks.explain: The scaling sweep showed MTP underperforming next-token training for small models and outperforming it at scale. The 12% figure is for the 13B model. Inference cost is unchanged when only the next-token head is used.

lessons.title: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain

blocks.md: DeepSeek-V3 (a 671B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, 37B active per token) adopted MTP, citing Gloeckle et al., but changed the design. Gloeckle's heads predict in parallel and independently. DeepSeek-V3 predicts additional tokens **sequentially** with small modules and keeps the **complete causal chain** at each prediction depth: the module predicting two tokens ahead also gets to see the token one ahead.

The $k$-th MTP module has four parts: the **shared** embedding layer, the **shared** output head (both reused from the main model), one transformer block $\mathrm{TRM}_k$, and a projection matrix $M_k$ of shape $d \times 2d$. For input position $i$ at depth $k$ it combines two vectors: the hidden state $h_i^{k-1}$ from the previous depth (the main model's final hidden state when $k = 1$), and the embedding of the token $t_{i+k}$.

blocks.caption: Equations 21 to 23 of the DeepSeek-V3 report. [a; b] is concatenation, so M_k projects 2d back to d. The output predicts token i + k + 1.

blocks.title: Main model plus one MTP module (D = 1)

scenes.caption: The main model is an ordinary next-token model: embed, 61 transformer layers, output head, loss on t(i+1).
The MTP module takes the main model's final hidden state h_i and normalizes it.
It also embeds the true next token t(i+1) with the shared embedding. This is the causal chain: the depth-1 prediction is conditioned on the token one step ahead.
The two d-vectors are concatenated and projected back to d by M_1, then pass through one extra transformer block TRM_1 (causal attention over the sequence).
The shared output head turns the result into a distribution for t(i+2). Embedding and head are physically shared with the main model, so the module adds only M_1, the block and its norms.

blocks.title: Index alignment for depth 1 on a 7-token sequence

scenes.caption: A 7-token training sequence.
The main model at position i predicts t(i+1): six targets, t2 to t7.
The depth-1 module at position i embeds the true token t(i+1) (teacher forcing) next to the main model's h_i.
And predicts t(i+2): five targets, t3 to t7. Positions 6 and 7 have no token two ahead. The report counts T inputs plus a final target t(T+1), so there the module runs on T - k positions.

blocks.md: The training objective adds the MTP losses to the main loss. Each depth $k$ has an ordinary cross-entropy $\mathcal{L}^k_{\text{MTP}}$ over its targets; these are averaged over the $D$ depths and scaled by a weight $\lambda$:

blocks.caption: Equation 25. DeepSeek-V3 uses D = 1, with lambda = 0.3 for the first 10T training tokens and 0.1 for the remaining 4.8T.

blocks.md: Concrete numbers from the released model: `num_nextn_predict_layers` is 1 in `config.json`, and the module is stored as layer 61, right after the main model's layers 0 to 60. The weights documentation lists 11.5B unique module parameters, excluding the shared embedding and output head (about 0.9B each; 129,280 x 7,168 = 0.93B). At inference the module can be dropped entirely, leaving the main model unchanged.

blocks.title: DeepSeek-V3 ablation: adding one MTP module (Table 4)

scenes.caption: Small MoE baseline (15.7B total, 1.33T tokens), no MTP.
Same model and data with a depth-1 MTP module: HumanEval +6.1, GSM8K +6.0, MATH +1.9, MBPP +1.0, MMLU +3.3 points. Inference cost is identical because the module is discarded.
Large MoE baseline (228.7B total, 540B tokens), no MTP.
With MTP: HumanEval +9.2, GSM8K +1.7, MATH +1.2, MBPP +0.6, but MMLU -0.9. 'Most benchmarks' improve, not all.

blocks.md: Parallel heads versus a sequential chain. In Gloeckle's design, head 3 must guess x(t+3) without knowing what x(t+1) and x(t+2) are. In DeepSeek-V3's design, depth k is told the true tokens up to t(i+k) during training, so each depth solves an ordinary one-step-further problem. The report notes the causal-chain idea resembles EAGLE, a speculative decoding method, but uses it to improve training.

blocks.question: At depth k = 2 in DeepSeek-V3's scheme, which inputs does the module use for position i, and which token does it predict?
options: h_i from the main model and Emb(t_i+1); predicts t_i+2
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+3); predicts t_i+3
Only Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
blocks.explain: Depth k combines h at depth k - 1 with the embedding of t(i+k) and predicts t(i+k+1). For k = 2 that is h from depth 1, Emb(t(i+2)), and target t(i+3).

blocks.question: Why did the DeepSeek-V3 ablation conclude that MTP improved the model itself rather than just adding capacity?
options: The MTP models had more active parameters at inference
The module was discarded at inference, so the evaluated networks had identical cost and shape
MTP models were trained on more tokens
Only benchmarks that MTP helped were reported
blocks.explain: During evaluation the MTP module is dropped, so baseline and MTP models run the same main network at the same cost. The difference comes from how the shared weights were trained. The table even includes a regression (MMLU at large scale).

lessons.title: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster

blocks.md: Decoding a large model is usually memory-bandwidth bound: each step reads all the weights to produce one token. **Speculative decoding** (Leviathan et al., 2023) uses a cheap draft to propose several tokens and the big model to check them all in one forward pass. MTP models carry their own drafter, the extra heads, so they can do this **without a separate draft model**. Gloeckle et al. use blockwise parallel decoding (Stern, Shazeer and Uszkoreit, 2018), which is greedy self-speculation.

The greedy rule is simple. The $n$ heads propose the next $n$ tokens, one each. Head 1's proposal is the main model's own greedy token, so it is always correct. The next forward pass runs the model on the drafted tokens; at each drafted position the next-token head says what it would have produced. Keep the drafts up to the first disagreement. Because the check uses the next-token head itself, the output is **identical** to ordinary greedy decoding with that head; only the number of forward passes changes.

scenes.caption: Context 'for i in'. One forward pass runs all four heads at the last position. (Illustrative tokens.)
The heads propose 'range', '(', 'n', ')'. Head 1's token 'range' is the true greedy token; the other three are guesses.
Next forward pass over the drafts. After 'range', head 1 says '(' (match). After '(', it says 'len', not 'n' (mismatch). Later drafts are discarded.
Emitted: 'range', '(' and head 1's correction 'len'. In that same pass, heads 2 to 4 at the '(' position already drafted the tokens after 'len', so the next cycle needs no extra pass.

blocks.md: How many tokens does each forward pass yield on average? A simplified model: suppose each draft after the first is accepted with probability $a$, independently, given that the previous ones were. With $k$ extra drafts the expected tokens per forward is a geometric sum.

blocks.tex: \mathbb{E}[\text{tokens per forward}] = 1 + a + a^2 + \dots + a^{k} = \frac{1 - a^{k+1}}{1 - a}
blocks.caption: Simplified: real acceptance rates differ by head and by context, and drafts are not independent. The first term 1 is the token the main head always contributes.

blocks.title: Expected tokens per forward pass vs acceptance rate

scenes.caption: One extra draft (DeepSeek-V3 with D = 1). Its report gives an 85% to 90% acceptance rate for the second token, which this model turns into 1.85 to 1.90 tokens per forward.
Two extra drafts: at a = 0.85 the model gives 2.57 tokens per forward. Each extra draft adds less, because it only counts if all earlier ones were accepted.
Three extra drafts (four heads): 3.19 at a = 0.85 and 3.44 at a = 0.9. The ceiling is 1 + k, reached only if every draft is accepted.

blocks.md: Measured numbers. Gloeckle et al. ran greedy self-speculative decoding on their 7B 4-token code model (prompts and 512-token completions from unseen test data, batch size 42). Using 2, 3 and 4 heads gave 1.94, 2.78 and 3.50 tokens per forward and relative speedups of 1.85x, 2.54x and 3.05x. For an 8-byte prediction byte-level model the speedup reached 6.4x. DeepSeek-V3 reports 1.8 times the tokens per second with its single MTP module.

blocks.title: Tokens per forward vs real speedup (Gloeckle Table S2, code)

scenes.caption: Tokens produced per forward pass. 3.50 with all four heads, out of a maximum of 4.
Wall-clock speedup is lower: 1.85x, 2.54x, 3.05x. A verifying pass processes several positions and runs extra heads, so it costs a bit more than a plain decode step (ratios 0.95, 0.91, 0.87).

blocks.prompt: Pretrained 4-token heads versus heads bolted on afterwards: which should draft better?
blocks.reveal: Pretrained heads. Gloeckle et al. note that pretraining with the multi-token loss makes the extra heads much more accurate than simply finetuning a next-token model, which unlocks the full speedup. **Medusa** (Cai et al., 2024) is the bolt-on approach: extra decoding heads trained on top of a frozen model (Medusa-1, over 2.2x) or jointly with it (Medusa-2, 2.3x to 3.6x), drafting several candidates per head and verifying them with tree attention.

blocks.md: Lossless means 'same output as greedy decoding with the next-token head'. With temperature sampling, accepting a draft needs the speculative sampling rule of Leviathan et al. to keep the output distribution exact; simply comparing argmax tokens would change it.

**Tradeoffs to keep in mind.**

- Training: extra head layers or modules cost compute and memory (DeepSeek-V3's module alone has 11.5B unique parameters), and the per-head memory schedule is needed to avoid the nV logit blow-up.
- Quality: gains depend on scale and data; small models, multiple-choice benchmarks and some natural-language settings show no gain or regressions, and $n$ needs tuning.
- Inference: drafting pays off when decoding is memory-bound. If a server is already compute-bound at large batch, extra verification work can eat the gain, so measure on your workload.

MTP gives two separate benefits: a training signal that can make the main model better, and heads that can draft tokens for exact, faster greedy decoding. You can use the first without the second by discarding the heads.

blocks.question: An MTP model with one extra draft has acceptance rate 0.9. Under the simplified independence model, about how many tokens does each forward pass yield, and why is the measured speedup lower?
options: 1.9 tokens; verification passes cost a little more than plain decode steps
2.0 tokens; the draft is always accepted at greedy temperature
1.81 tokens, because 0.9 squared is 0.81
1.9 tokens; the speedup is lower because outputs differ from greedy decoding
blocks.explain: Expected tokens = 1 + a = 1.9. The wall-clock gain is smaller because each verifying pass processes extra positions and runs the drafter. Output does not differ: greedy verification reproduces greedy decoding exactly. DeepSeek-V3 reports 85% to 90% acceptance and 1.8x tokens per second.

blocks.question: You serve a Gloeckle-style 4-token model with greedy decoding and enable self-speculative decoding with all 4 heads. What happens to the generated text?
options: It becomes more diverse because heads 2 to 4 inject their own choices
It is identical to greedy decoding with head 1; only the number of forward passes drops
It is identical only if every draft is accepted
It degrades slightly, which is the price of a 3x speedup
blocks.explain: Every emitted token is one that head 1 would have chosen given the same prefix: drafts are kept only when they match head 1's prediction, and the first mismatch is replaced by head 1's token. Acceptance rate changes speed, never content.
